opening_message:
Ticket 1: Dominic Taylor (employee ID E004) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E004.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Dominic Taylor (E004) is a full-time Engineer. Requested write access to Source Code, owned by the Engineer role. Full-time employees may have up to write, and the role owns the system, so write is within policy.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E004 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since training is basic, maximum is read. Requested write exceeds max, so recommend read.
reason: The two team notes conflict on Dominic Taylor's (E004) employment status: the HR note says full-time Engineer (which would permit write access to Source Code, owned by the Engineer role), while the Security note says contractor with basic security training (which limits access to read; write requires advanced training for contractors). Given the conflicting records, I cannot confirm that E004 is eligible for write access. I grant the most restrictive level that is safe under either interpretation: read.

1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If Dominic is a full-time Engineer, max is write (and role owns system so admin possible). Requested write is within policy → grant write.

If Dominic is a contractor with basic training, max is read → grant read.
